sections.h2: Which Lawrenceburg offices touch an Anderson County tax bill?
sections.html:
The Sheriff's counter, 208 S Main St, takes the money. Questions go to (502) 839-4021, Monday through Friday, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. The Property Valuation Administrator, (502) 839-4061, decides the assessment behind each bill. Alton, McBrayer and the other crossroads places in this 202-square-mile county use the same two offices as Lawrenceburg, the only city.

Bills leave the Sheriff's Office in the final days of September and money is accepted starting October 1. Lenders are no longer mailed copies, meaning a borrower paying through escrow ought to ask the servicer in October if it holds a copy.

Richard Clough Anderson Jr., a legislator and later U.S. minister to Colombia, gave the county its name. A General Assembly act of January 28, 1854 changed the line between Anderson and Franklin counties, so owners near that edge can ask the PVA to confirm which county bills the parcel.

sections.h2: How fast does an unpaid Anderson County bill grow?
sections.html:
On its tax page the Sheriff publishes the statewide schedule from KRS 134.015. The accepted forms are cash, check and money order. Installments are refused, and a postmark earns nothing because the office needs the funds in hand by the date.

Anderson County Sheriff tax bill stages with the effect on the amount owed (andersoncountysheriff.com)
StageDatesEffect on the amount
EarlyOctober 1 to November 12 percent discount
PlainNovember 2 to December 31The printed amount
First penaltyJanuary 1 to 31Five percent on top
Second penaltyFebruary 1 until the office shuts on April 15Ten percent, plus ten percent more as the Sheriff's fee

Consider a made-up $2,000 bill. It costs $1,960 in the discount month, $2,000 in November and December, and $2,100 in January. From February the state's own sample shows the add-on being figured on the tax plus penalty, so the bill becomes $2,000 plus $200 plus $220, or $2,420. From best month to worst the gap is $460.

After that last day the bill is no longer the Sheriff's problem. At the County Clerk it turns into a certificate of delinquency. The Sheriff's page lists the extras: 20 percent for the County Attorney, 10 percent for the Clerk, and 1 percent interest each month. Summer can bring a sale to an outside buyer.

sections.h2: What does a $1,000 bill turn into at the clerk's counter?
sections.html:
Kentucky's revenue agency offers a model. A $1,000 bill, once the 10 percent penalty, the Sheriff's add-on and an assumed 4 percent commission are included, reaches the clerk at $1,254. Paid in five business days it comes to $1,387.79, and after the county attorney's first notice, $1,611.30. Commission rates differ by county, so get a real payoff figure from the clerk.

The first letter goes out within a month of the handoff. KRS 134.128 puts the tax sale between 90 and 135 days after the transfer, with advertising in print and online.

The Sheriff handles everything until April 15. Afterward the clerk's website has a lookup called DTax for delinquent taxes. Its page says the data is informational and the clerk alone decides the actual dollar amount for each bill at the time of any sale. An owner with an old balance should obtain a written payoff from the office and not rely on a screen.

sections.h2: Is it worth contesting a valuation in Anderson County?
sections.html:
The order is fixed. Assessments speak as of January 1. The roll is open for 13 days from the first Monday of May. A meeting with the PVA or a deputy must happen first, and the County Clerk accepts the appeal through the next day after inspection ends.

About a month after inspection closes (25 to 35 days) the local appeals board meets, for five days at most. It expects paper: proof of the land and structures, insurance coverage, building costs and comparable listings. A bare filing loses. Staying home from the hearing ends the appeal, and a final value over your claim means an extra bill.

sections.h2: Does an Anderson County senior pay less?
sections.html:
The PVA takes homestead applications from owners who have turned 65 and from owners classified as totally disabled. For 2025 and 2026 the state subtracts $49,100 from assessed value, a figure reset every other year. On a house assessed at $225,100 it would leave $176,000 to tax.

Age is shown with a birth certificate, license or passport. A disability claim is renewed yearly unless the owner is a service-connected disabled veteran or has been found permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

sections.h2: What has population growth done to Anderson County housing?
sections.html:
Anderson County had 4,520 residents in 1830, fell from 7,404 in 1860 to 5,449 in 1870, then rose to 14,571 in 1990 and 23,852 in 2020. An estimate for mid-2025 reads 25,225. Wikipedia calls it the ninth fastest-growing and 48th most populated of Kentucky's counties. Residents had a median age of 42.0 in 2020, and just over half (56.8 percent) lived in areas the Census counts as urban.

Houses follow people: the county held 10,652 housing units in July 2025, and builders took out 147 permits in 2025. Owners can compare their assessments with recent neighborhood sales before the roll opens.

About 90.4 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, and 94.5 percent of households have a computer, so most owners can look up a parcel online or call the PVA without much trouble.

  • Half of owner-occupied homes were valued above $225,100 (2020 to 2024 survey).
  • Households that own: 77.6 percent of 9,653.
  • Midpoint household income: $74,488; midpoint gross rent: $927.
  • Owners paid a median $1,391 a month with a mortgage and $411 without one.

Someone who bought last year can list the deed price as next January's value if the home is unchanged.

In 2023 the county held 352 employer establishments with 4,175 jobs and $189.3 million in payroll. Shops sold $338.8 million in 2022. Some 60.2 percent of residents over 16 work or look for work, and the average trip to work takes 30.4 minutes.

Among adults, 90.5 percent have a high school diploma and 26.2 percent a bachelor's degree or higher. Broadband reaches 88.7 percent of households, 1,350 residents are veterans, and 22.0 percent are children.

The 2020 count found 9,369 households and 10,044 housing units, of which 6.7 percent stood vacant. Rental vacancy was 3.8 percent against 1.3 percent for owned homes, and 22.4 percent of households were headed by a woman with no partner present.

Alongside the 352 employer establishments, the county had 1,788 nonemployer businesses in 2024 and 427 employer firms in 2023, 99 of them owned by women. Households average 2.51 people. Building permits fell from the 192 Wikipedia lists for 2022 to 147 in 2025.

sections.h2: How do I clear back taxes before selling?
sections.html:
• The Sheriff can quote the live balance, earlier years included. After April 15 ask the Clerk.
  • Have the closing agent clear arrears out of your share and record the release.
  • The deed must show where the buyer's tax bill goes (KRS 382.135).
  • Anyone with a homestead exemption should tell the PVA about the sale.

Behind on taxes and unwilling to make repairs? Request a written cash offer. Taxes and clerk charges are taken from the price at closing.

faqs.q: Until what date does the discount last?
faqs.a: Through November 1. KRS 134.015 gives 2 percent off to a taxpayer paying in full by then. Between November 2 and year end the printed amount applies.

faqs.q: What happens if I wait until February?
faqs.a: Between February 1 and April 15 the Sheriff adds a 10 percent penalty and another 10 percent as an add-on fee.

faqs.q: Can I pay in two halves?
faqs.a: No. Partial payments are not taken, and a check that arrives after the cutoff counts as late whatever its postmark.

faqs.q: Where does an objection to my value begin?
faqs.a: Ask the PVA's office for a conference. The County Clerk cannot accept an appeal without one, and the filing deadline falls on the workday after inspection ends.

faqs.q: How big is the homestead break?
faqs.a: For the 2025 and 2026 years it removes $49,100 from the assessed value. Applications go to the PVA.
